content: Silphium laciniatum, commonly known as Compass Flower, Compass Plant, or Rosinweed, is a species of flowering plant that belongs to the genus Silphium. It is indigenous to east-central North America, with its range extending from southern Ontario and New York in the north, down to Alabama in the south, and westward across the prairies to North Dakota and Colorado, reaching as far south as Texas. This plant is a perennial herbaceous species that bears a resemblance to sunflowers. It typically grows to a height of 1 to 4 meters and features stems that are covered in bristly hairs. The leaves of the plant are alternately arranged along the stem and are deeply lobed in a pinnate fashion. The basal leaves can reach lengths of up to 40 centimeters, while the leaves higher up the stem are progressively smaller. The flowers of Silphium laciniatum are borne in flower heads, or capitula, which measure 5 to 12 centimeters in diameter. These flower heads consist of a ring of ray florets encircling a central disc of florets that is approximately 2 to 3 centimeters in diameter. The plant typically blooms in late summer, with flowering occurring from July to September. The name Compass Plant is derived from the unique orientation of its foliage, which tends to align in a north-south direction. This alignment minimizes the surface area exposed to the intense heat of the midday sun. The plant is equipped with a deep taproot, which can extend to depths of more than 9 to 14 feet. This extensive root system makes the plant highly resilient and capable of withstanding drought conditions. Historically, the Compass Plant was utilized in Native American herbal medicine. It was employed as a vermifuge to expel intestinal parasites and was also used to treat respiratory conditions such as coughs and asthma.
